statement: If an odd number be prime to any number, it will also be prime to the double of it.
heath_proof: For let the odd number A be prime to any number B, and let C be double of B; I say that A is prime to C. For, if they are not prime to one another, some number will measure them. Let a number measure them, and let it be D. Now A is odd; therefore D is also odd. And since D which is odd measures C, and C is even, therefore [D] will measure the half of C also. [IX. 30] But B is half of C; therefore D measures B. But it also measures A; therefore D measures A, B which are prime to one another: which is impossible. Therefore A cannot but be prime to C. Therefore A, C are prime to one another.

9.31
**Statement:** If an odd number be prime to any number, it will also be prime to the double of it.

**Step 1.** Let A be an odd number, let A be prime to any number B, and let C be double of B, so that C is made up of B and B. I say that A is also prime to C.

**Step 2.** Suppose, if possible, that A and C are not prime to one another. Then A and C are not measured by an unit alone as a common measure [D7.12], so some number D (other than an unit) measures both A and C.

**Step 3.** I say that D is odd. For, since D measures A, A is a multiple of D [D7.5], that is, A is made up of D taken some number of times, so A is the sum of numbers each equal to D. If D were even, A would be a sum of even numbers (or D itself, if taken once), and therefore A would be even [9.21], that is, divisible into two equal parts [D7.6]. But A is odd, that is, not divisible into two equal parts [D7.7]; which is impossible. Therefore D is not even, so D is odd.

**Step 4.** Now C, being made up of the two equal parts B and B, is divisible into two equal parts, and so C is even [D7.6], and the half of C is B.

**Step 5.** Since the odd number D measures the even number C, D also measures the half of C [9.30]; that is, D measures B.

**Step 6.** But D also measures A. Therefore the number D, which is not an unit, measures both A and B, so A and B are not measured by an unit alone as a common measure; hence A and B are not prime to one another [D7.12]. But by hypothesis A is prime to B; which is absurd.

**Step 7.** Therefore A and C are not measured by any number other than an unit as a common measure, so A and C are prime to one another [D7.12]. Hence, if an odd number be prime to any number, it is also prime to the double of it. Q.E.D.
